summary: Defines an extension to CoAP that lets a client observe a resource: it gets the current state and then receives updates from the server as the state changes. The approach is best-effort and suits constrained devices and networks.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking a thermometer again and again, you ask it to tell you whenever the temperature changes.

questions: how to subscribe to resource updates in coap
what does observe option 0 mean in coap
what is max-age in coap notifications
how do i stop observing a coap resource
subtitle: Ask a CoAP server once and get told whenever a resource changes, without polling.

tldr.problem: A CoAP client that wants a current copy of a resource over time has to keep asking for it, and repeated polling or HTTP long polling costs too much complexity and overhead for constrained devices.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a GET with the Observe Option set to 0 to register. The server keeps a list of observers and sends further responses, called notifications, carrying the client's token and a sequence number whenever the state changes.
tldr.outcome: Delivery is best-effort with eventual consistency, and every notification carries a Max-Age. RFC 7641 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8323.

today: RFC 7641 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8323. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and the Observer Pattern
sections.content:
CoAP (RFC 7252) offers RESTful services like HTTP, but for highly constrained nodes and networks. In the REST model a client asks and the server answers with the state of the resource at that moment. That does not suit a client that wants a current copy over a period of time. Polling and HTTP long polling add complexity or overhead that constrained environments cannot afford.

RFC 7641 extends CoAP using the observer design pattern. The subject is a resource on a server, and the observer is a client. The client registers with an extended GET request, and the server adds it to the list of observers. Each change produces a notification, an additional response to that one request with a complete, updated representation. The RFC does not try to replace publish/subscribe systems or to solve everything HTTP solutions solve.
sections.eli5: It is like asking a friend to text you whenever the weather changes, instead of calling every five minutes to ask.

sections.title: Consistency and Observable Resources
sections.content:
The goal is to keep the client's view as close as possible to the real state, but the two will sometimes differ: there is latency, notifications can be lost, and the server may wrongly decide the client is no longer interested. So the protocol is best-effort, limited by congestion control, and a client cannot expect to see every state. Each notification is labelled with a maximum age up to which a mismatch is acceptable, and the design follows eventual consistency: if a resource stops changing, all registered observers eventually get the latest state.

The protocol has no way to set triggers or thresholds. The server decides what its observable resources are. A temperature sensor could expose a resource that changes every few seconds, one that changes to COLD or WARM at thresholds, or a parameterized one such as /temperature/critical?above=42. The application designer picks the right level of complexity.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a text arrives late or gets lost, so the news can be a little old. Each text says how old is too old, and if things go quiet, you finally get the last news.

sections.title: The Observe Option
sections.content:
The Observe Option is option number 6. Its format is uint and its length is 0 to 3 bytes. It is elective, not critical for processing the request, and it is not part of the Cache-Key.

In a GET request, value 0 means register and 1 means deregister. The list entry is made from the client endpoint and the client's token. If the server cannot or will not add an entry, the request falls back to a normal GET and the response has no Observe Option, which tells the client it must poll.

In a response, the option marks the message as a notification and its value is a sequence number used to detect reordering. Notifications usually have the response code 2.05 (Content). If the client sent ETag Options, a notification can be 2.03 (Valid) with no payload.
sections.eli5: The option is a little sticker on the message. On a request, 0 means start telling me, and 1 means stop. On an answer, it is a number that shows how new the answer is.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
A client MUST NOT register more than once for the same target resource, and it MUST aggregate such requests. A notification carries the client's token and uses the same Content-Format as the initial response. If the resource changes so that a normal GET would give a non-2.xx response (for example 4.04 Not Found), the server sends that response, without an Observe Option, and removes the client from the list. Notification order among clients is undefined.

For freshness, the server MUST give a Max-Age in each notification. When a notification's age passes its Max-Age, the client MUST NOT assume it reflects the real state and can send a new GET with the same token. The client SHOULD wait a random time between 5 and 15 seconds after Max-Age expires. For reordering, the server sets the Observe value to the 24 least significant bits of a strictly increasing sequence number, which must not rise by more than 2^23 in under 256 seconds. The client treats the most recently sent notification as freshest, using the comparison in the RFC, which also accepts a notification more than 128 seconds newer.

To stop, a client can ignore the next notification so that it answers with a Reset message, or explicitly send a GET with Observe set to 1.
sections.eli5: Each note has a number so you can put late ones in the right order, and an expiry so you know when to stop trusting it. To stop the notes, you can ignore them until the sender gives up, or you can say stop.

sections.title: Sending Notifications Without Causing Congestion
sections.content:
A notification can be confirmable or non-confirmable, chosen by the server for each one. A client that acknowledges a confirmable notification shows it is still interested. A Reset, or a timeout on the last retransmission, means the server MUST remove the entry. A server that mostly sends non-confirmable notifications MUST send a confirmable one at least every 24 hours.

Because one request can produce unlimited notifications, the server carries responsibility for congestion control. It MUST limit outstanding notifications to a client to NSTART (1 by default). It SHOULD NOT send more than one non-confirmable notification per round-trip time on average, or, with no RTT estimate, more than one every 3 seconds.

The server MAY skip intermediate states, but MUST ensure the client eventually sees the latest state. It MAY also supersede an outstanding transmission with a new notification that has the current state.
sections.eli5: The sender must not flood you with messages. It sends one at a time, may skip old news, and asks now and then whether you are still there.

sections.title: Intermediaries and Web Linking
sections.content:
A client talks to the first intermediary, such as a proxy, as if it were the server. The intermediary SHOULD register with the next hop using this protocol, and each pair of hops is independent: each generates its own Observe values and sets Max-Age from the age of its local copy. If two or more clients want the same resource, the intermediary MUST register only once and fan out the notifications. That helps scalability.

A link to a CoAP resource MAY carry the attribute obs. It is only a hint that the resource is useful to observe, with no value, and it is not a promise that the Observe Option will work.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle can listen for many people at once and pass the news on, so the far-away sensor only has to talk to one listener.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Observing can greatly worsen amplification attacks, because notifications may be larger than the request and there can be many of them. Without client authentication, a server MUST strictly limit the notifications it sends between acknowledgements, so non-confirmable notifications MUST be interspersed with confirmable ones.

Stale data can be a threat, so clients must not use a representation after its Max-Age expires. Attackers may try to exhaust the observer list, so servers may apply access controls and can fall back to a plain GET. Intermediaries must make sure notifications cannot form a loop, and caches are a simple way to break loops. With DTLS (the coaps scheme), all notifications MUST be returned within the same epoch of the same connection as the request.
sections.eli5: A bad guy could trick the sensor into sending lots of messages to a victim. So the sensor must check now and then that someone really wants them.
